input: This study presents a comparison of two forms of a copper-zinc oxide catalyst, a structured form and a pellet form, for the reaction of carbon dioxide and hydrogen to methanol. All of the experiments were performed at 250 °C and 50 bar, with a feed ratio H2/CO2 = 3 and a single, fixed feed composition. The performance of each form was assessed in terms of space-time yield, which is defined as the mass of product produced per unit catalyst volume per hour, along with the pressure drop across the bed and the loss of activity with time on stream. The structured catalyst recorded a space-time yield of 0.68 kg L-1 h-1 and a pressure drop of 0.18 bar, while the pellet catalyst recorded a space-time yield of 0.38 kg L-1 h-1 together with a pressure drop of 1.48 bar. With regard to stability, the activity loss after 100 h was 7% in the case of the structured catalyst and 14% in the case of the pellet catalyst. Overall, the structured form can be seen to deliver a higher yield at a lower pressure drop under the conditions studied, and it also deactivates more slowly. It should nevertheless be noted that the comparison is restricted to the one feed composition employed here, and that no sulfur-bearing feed was tested. Yield and pressure drop are, moreover, seldom reported for the same catalyst charge, which limits the comparisons that can be drawn with other published work.
target: Carbon dioxide and hydrogen react over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst to give methanol. The catalyst was tested in a structured form and a pellet form at 250 °C and 50 bar, with a feed ratio H2/CO2 = 3 and one feed composition. Space-time yield (the mass of product per unit catalyst volume per hour) was 0.68 kg L-1 h-1 for the structured catalyst and 0.38 kg L-1 h-1 for the pellet catalyst. The yield is stated per unit catalyst volume, so the two forms are compared on the volume each charge occupies. Pressure drop was 0.18 bar for the structured catalyst and 1.48 bar for the pellet catalyst. Activity loss after 100 h was 7% for the structured catalyst and 14% for the pellet catalyst. At the stated conditions the structured form gives the higher yield at the lower pressure drop, and its activity falls more slowly over the test; the pellet form's lower yield is not accompanied by a lower pressure drop. The comparison is limited to the one feed composition tested, at the stated temperature and pressure throughout, and no sulfur-bearing feed was tested at any point. Yield and pressure drop are seldom reported for the same catalyst charge, and the paired values are stated together here so that both comparisons rest on the same test.
